# Open-source electrophilic fragment screening platform to identify chemical starting points for UCHL1 covalent inhibitors

**Authors:** Scott B. Ficarro; Zachary H. Marto; Nicholas M. Girardi; Dingyu Deng; Isabella Jaen Maisonet; Guillaume Adelmant; Laura E. Fleming; Mona Sharafi; Isidoro Tavares; Andrew Zhao; HyoJeon Kim; Hyuk-Soo Seo; Sirano Dhe-Paganon; Sara J. Buhrlage; Jarrod A. Marto

## Abstract

Target-based screening of covalent fragment libraries with mass spectrometry has emerged as a powerful strategy to identify chemical starting points for small molecule inhibitors or find new binding pockets on proteins of interest. These libraries span diverse chemical space with a modest number of compounds. Screening covalent fragments against purified protein targets reduces the demands on the mass spectrometer with respect to absolute throughput, detection limit, and dynamic range. Given these relaxed analytical requirements, we sought to develop an open-source, medium-throughput mass spectrometry system for target-based covalent fragment screening. Our platform comprises automated, dual LC desalting columns integrated with electrospray ionization for rapid sample introduction and mass spectrometry detection. The system is operated through a simple Python graphical user interface running on commodity microcontroller boards which allow integration with diverse liquid chromatography and mass spectrometry instruments. We provide scripts for fragment pooling, construction of sample batches, along with routines for data processing and visualization. The system enables primary screening of ~10,000 covalent fragments per day in pooled format. In a proof-of-concept study we executed primary and secondary screens to identify 27 hit fragments against UCHL1, a deubiquitinating enzyme that is emerging as a drug target of interest across multiple clinical indications. We validated and triaged these covalent compounds through a series of orthogonal biochemical and chemoproteomic assays. The most promising chloroacetamide covalent fragment inhibited UCHL1 activity in vitro (IC50 < 5 μM) and exhibited dose-dependent binding along with good selectivity against 57 cellular DUBs as quantified by activity-based protein profiling.

## Introduction

Systematic studies spanning DNA sequencing, functional genomics, and integrated analysis of multi-omic data continue to highlight new targets in well-established druggable enzymes [1–6], as well as gene families such as the deubiquitinating enzymes (DUBs) that have more recently emerged as potential disease drivers [7–9]. There are approximately 100 human DUBs that catalyze cleavage of ubiquitin and ubiquitin-like (UBL) post-translational marks from substrate proteins [10]. As key members of the ubiquitin proteasome system (UPS), DUBs are functionally involved in numerous cellular processes. DUBs are classified into seven sub-families based on sequence homology with most functioning as cysteine proteases. The Ubiquitin Carboxy-Terminal Hydrolase L1 (UCHL1) is a small protein (~28 kDa) in the UCH sub-family [11]. UCHL1 is thought to stabilize the cellular pool of ubiquitin by binding free, monomeric ubiquitin, while also deubiquitinating other substrates, including endogenous peptides and metabolites. UCHL1 is very abundant in neuronal tissues, has limited expression in most other healthy tissues, but is over-expressed in several cancers. Accordingly, UCHL1 loss-of-function is linked to neurodegenerative disorders [12,13] while increased activity, primarily through increased protein abundance, is thought to play a role in multiple cancers [14].

Recent clinical success has driven renewed interest in covalent drugs [15,16]. Compared to their reversible counterparts, covalent inhibitors provide high efficacy at lower concentration and less frequent dosing, complete target inhibition, with activity restored only after de novo synthesis of new protein, and wider tolerance for pharmacokinetic parameters. Building on chemotypes reported in the patent literature [17], we [18] and others [19–22] have used complementary approaches to characterize diverse N-cyanopyrrolidines and chloroacetohydrazides as covalent inhibitors of UCHL1. Together, these studies establish the chemical tractability of UCHL1 for pharmacologic inhibition although the reported compounds performed unevenly with respect to their on- and off-target activity profiles. Collectively, these results inspired us to consider alternative approaches to diversify chemical starting points for UCHL1 inhibitory compounds.

Covalent fragment screening is gaining momentum as a powerful strategy to identify chemical starting points or find new binding pockets on protein targets [23–29]. Compared to diversity compound collections often used with traditional high-throughput screening (HTS) approaches, covalent fragments provide efficient coverage of chemical space with smaller libraries [30]. Irreversible binding driven by mild electrophile groups enables rigorous characterization of covalent modification by mass spectrometry with overall fragment activity profiles mediated by a balance of warhead reactivity and non-covalent interactions with the protein target. Recent advances now provide functionalized fragment libraries [31], to facilitate selectivity profiling and target deconvolution in complex proteomes, as well as covalent warheads that target other (e.g., non-cysteine) amino acids [32–37], thereby extending the reach of fragment screening. Use of purified protein and covalent compound libraries for target-based fragment screening reduces the demands on the mass spectrometer with respect to absolute throughput, detection limit, and dynamic range. We reasoned that these somewhat relaxed analytical criteria would provide an opportunity to utilize an open-source hardware/software approach [38, 39] to circumvent the high cost, proprietary, and manufacture-specific nature of commercial mass spectrometry screening systems. Our platform is based on rapid hardware/software prototyping and comprises automated pick-up of protein-ligand conjugates from well-plates followed by injection onto parallelized dual desalting columns integrated with electrospray ionization for mass spectrometry detection. The system is operated through a simple Python graphical user interface running on microcontroller boards and agnostically integrates with diverse liquid chromatography and mass spectrometry instruments through a simple contact closure. To facilitate broad adoption [40], we provide a detailed parts manifest, production and assembly instructions, as well as software for instrument operation and data analysis. The system enables a primary screen throughput of ~10,000 covalent fragments per day in pooled format. As a powerful proof-of-concept, we screened purified UCHL1 against a library of 4200 covalent fragments and identified 41 hits. We re-screened these fragments as singletons and validated 27 of them as UCHL1 covalent binders. Through a series of orthogonal biochemical and chemoproteomic validation assays we identified 5 fragments that inhibited UCHL1 enzymatic activity and modified the catalytic cysteine residue. Our lead compound exhibited dose-dependent binding for UCHL1 with good selectivity across endogenous DUBs by activity-based protein profiling.

## Methods

### Open source hardware, electronics, and software

Instrument hardware was designed in Sketchup Pro (2024, Trimble; Supplementary Fig. 1). The frame consisted of OpenBuilds (https://openbuildspartstore.com/) aluminum V-slot assembled using T-nuts and brackets, with castors (Grainger) added for system mobility. Aluminum extrusion was cut to length according to the specifications using a residential grade compound miter saw and compatible non-ferrous metal blade. The 3-axis sample injector was based on an Openbuilds C-beam machine CNC system and assembled according to manufacturer instructions. Linear motion along X, Y, and Z axes was achieved with lead screw actuators each driven by a dedicated NEMA-23 stepper motor. The syringe pump was driven by a separate C-beam machine X-axis and NEMA-23 stepper motor. Each stepper motor was controlled with a DMT-542 stepper motor driver (www.omc-stepperonline.com/). The stepper motor drivers were controlled through Arduino-Unos loaded with grbl2arduino. One Arduino controlled the 3-axis autosampler gantry and a second Arduino-Uno controlled the syringe pump. A Python script (RobotControl.py) running on a Raspberry Pi controlled the Arduino-Unos as well as timing for contact closures for the system valve position (sample flow path control), LC (initiate organic gradient), and mass spectrometer (start acquisition). To organize and stabilize electronic connections amongst platform components, we designed (Autodesk Eagle) a custom printed circuit board (PCB, Osh Park) that accepted a 48 pin header from the Pi and routed 6-pin IDC connectors for each valve as well as a dedicated connection for each contact closure. We used wxPython to build a simple GUI for system control. Supplementary Fig. 2 shows overall electronics layout, with a BOM provided in Supplementary Table 1. We provide PCB files, Open-SCAD files for 3D printed parts, and Python code as Supplementary Material.

### Model proteins

Cytochrome C (equine) and enolase (yeast) were obtained from Sigma. Proteins were dissolved in PBS and protein concentration was measured by BCA.

### UCHL1 expression and purification

GST-tag construct of full length human UCHL1 (residues 1–223; gift from Dr. Chunxiang Wu) was overexpressed in E. coli BL21 (DE3) and purified using affinity chromatography and size-exclusion chromatography. Briefly, cells were grown at 37 °C in TB medium in the presence of 100 μg/mL of ampicillin to an OD of 0.8, cooled to 17 °C, induced with 400 μM isopropyl-1-thio-D-galactopyranoside (IPTG), incubated overnight for 20 h at 17 °C, collected by centrifugation, and stored at −80 °C. Cell pellets were lysed in buffer A (25 mM HEPES, pH 7.5, 200 mM NaCl, 5 % glycerol, and 0.5 mM TCEP) using Microfluidizer (Microfluidics), and the resulting lysate was centrifuged at 30,000 g for 40 min. Glutathione beads (GSH-sepharose, Cytiva) were mixed with cleared lysate for 90 min and washed with buffer A. Beads were transferred to an FPLC-compatible column, and the bound protein was washed further with buffer A for 10 column volumes and eluted with buffer B (25 mM HEPES, pH 7.5, 200 mM NaCl, 5 % glycerol, 0.5 mM TCEP, and 15 mM glutathione). The eluted sample was concentrated and purified further using a Superdex 200 16/600 column (Cytiva) in buffer A. GST-3C protease was added to SEC fractions, containing GST-UCHL1, and incubate overnight at 4 °C. GST-tag was removed by applying to a second glutathione bead column and purified further using a Superdex 75 16/600 column (Cytiva) in buffer A. The eluant containing cleaved UCHL1 was concentrated to ~30 mg/mL and stored in −80 °C. UCHL3 was prepared similarly.

### Injection scheme and LC–MS

The system utilized a total of 5 valves to parallelize two sample flow paths. Supplementary Fig. 3 shows the configuration of three low pressure, 6-port and two high pressure (one 6-port and one 10-port) valves. Proteins were eluted from each column with a 30-s HPLC gradient (Supplementary Table 2) that ramped from 0 to 100 % B in 24 s, followed by a linear ramp down to 0 % B in 6 s. We incorporated a 7 s delay to allow valve switching and pressure stabilization before launching the next gradient, for an inject-to-inject time of 37 s. Solvent A comprised 0.2 M acetic acid; solvent B comprised 60 % acetonitrile, 20 % isopropyl alcohol, 20 % n-propyl alcohol, and 0.2 M Acetic Acid. To inject the protein fragment samples, a 360 × 200 μm fused silica needle was positioned into the specified well and aspirated using the syringe actuator, placing the sample plug at the center of the 100 μL loop that spanned two ports of the 10-port valve. Actuating the 10-port valve placed the sample loop into the active flow path, and a single channel LC pump (Shizmadzu) pushed the sample plug onto one of the columns at a flow rate of 0.5 mL/min. Protein fragment samples were eluted from the column with a binary LC system (Shizmadzu). Between injections, the fused silica needle and flowpaths are rinsed with PBS that is collected into a waste container. Supplementary Fig. 4 illustrates the interleaved injection scheme which runs repeatedly until all wells of the reaction plate are analyzed.

### Fragment screening

Covalent fragments were obtained from Enamine (Monmouth Jct., NJ, 3200 compounds, “Cysteine focused Covalent Fragments library CYS-3200-50-Y-20) and ChemDiv (San Diego, CA, 1000 compounds selected from “Cysteine Targeting Covalent Ligand Library” based on criteria listed in Supplementary Methods). Both vendors supplied csv files with compound identifiers, plate ID, well, smiles, MW, and warhead. Warheads were grouped according to their type using vendor specific designations. For example, Enamine labeled chloroacetamides as ’Covalent3 - ClAcAmide_base’ and ’Covalent2 - ClAcAmide_nobase’ whereas ChemDiv used ’CL_AC’. These groups were used by Create-ScreenPools.py to pool only compounds of similar warhead type, for example: Categories [ ‘ Chloroacetamides ′ ] = [ ‘ Covalent 3 − ClAcAmide _ base ′ , ‘ Covalent 2 − − ClAcAmide _ nobase ′ , ‘ CL _ AC ′ ]

A liquid handler (i7, Beckman Coulter) was then used to pool equal volumes of ≤5 compounds based on the output CreateScreenPools.py using the Span-8 pipettor. For wells having <5 compounds, DMSO was added to keep concentrations and volumes the same. A total of 3 master pool plates were created, (1) acrylamides and cyanoacrylamides, (2) chloroacetamides and chloroketones, and (3) other. Dilutions of the 3 master pool plates were then produced using the 96-well pipetting head of the i7 liquid handler (384 wells accessed in quadrants i.e. upper left, upper right, lower left, lower right).

Screening reactions were performed by using the i7 to distribute UCHL1 from a quarter reservoir (20 mL capacity) across 3 × 384-well plates (1 μg per well, 40 μL, ~10 min. transfer time, span 8 probe) to match appropriately diluted pool plates (each of up to five compounds having a final concentration of 500 μM). We used the same platform to stamp 1 μL from 384 well dilution plates to corresponding wells of the protein plates. After 2 h, we used the liquid handler to quench each reaction well with 5 μL of 1 % formic acid, and mix. Plates were stored at −80 °C until analysis. Although less convenient, it should be noted that pooling, dilution, protein distribution, reactions, and quenching can also be performed manually with a 12-channel multichannel pipettor (odds, evens format). Sample lists were created for the mass spectrometer using ScreenPoolNamingWizard.py. User can select which screening plate is being interrogated, enter date, protein, datafile path, and MS method, and generate a csv file which can be imported into XCalibur software. Pool numbers are encoded into the datafile names for processing by FragmentScreen.py, which automated the analysis of the data files. This program utilizes Unidec [41] and the Multiplierz [42] toolkit to directly read and process native mass spectrometry data files to generate intact protein mass spectra along with an assessment of single-versus multi-covalent labeling and an estimate of fragment binding stoichiometry. FragmentScreen.py outputs graphically annotated PowerPoint slides to facilitate manual interpretation and figure generation, as well as a SQL file to support programmatic analysis or integration with other structure-based or chemi-informatic software tools. Scripts and auxiliary files are included in Supplementary material as Open-SourceHarwareSoftware.zip.

### Ubiquitin rhodamine 110 kinetic assay

The inhibitory activity of each covalent hit fragment on UCHL1 was evaluated using the ubiquitin rhodamine 110 kinetic assay. All assays were performed at 2 nM UCHL1 and 200 nM ubiquitin rhodamine 110 (Boston Biochem) in 50 mM Tris pH 8.0, 50 mM NaCl, and 0.02 % Tween20 in 384-well plates (Corning). The assay was initiated with the addition of ubiquitin rhodamine 110. Kinetic fluorescence data were collected every 30 s over a 30-min period (excitation and emission at 480 nm and 535 nm, respectively) on a BMG LABTECH CLARIOstar Microplate Reader. Initial velocities (RFU/min) were extracted and plotted against Log[fragment, μM]. IC50 values were derived using GraphPad Prism (non-linear regression: log(inhibitor) vs. response (three parameters)). Initially, fragments were tested on an eight-point dose-response curve (3.13–200 μM) with a two-hour incubation with UCHL1 at room temperature, with the assay repeated two times for each fragment (n = 2). Inhibitory compounds were then re-analyzed with twelve-point dose-response curves (400 nM - 400 μM) each repeated four times (n = 4), except for Z203045204 which was re-analyzed over a range of 100 nM–600 μM (n = 4). SB-1-F22, “F22” is a positive control compound [17] and was analyzed over a range of 4 nM–4 μM.

### In vitro target engagement

UCHL1 protein in PBS was incubated with each covalent fragment at the indicated concentration for 2 h at room temperature and then coincubated with a 10-fold molar excess of ubiquitin activity probe (ABP; 1:1 mix of biotin-Ub-PA and biotin-Ub-VME; UbiQ, Amsterdam, Netherlands) for 2 h at room temperature. Proteins were resolved by SDS-PAGE and visualized by Coomassie staining. Gels were imaged on a Bio Rad Gel Doc XR+ (white epi illumination, white light conversion screen, 60 s exposure). Signal for Ub-ABP bound UCHL1 relative to DMSO control was determined by densitometry with ImageJ software [43]. Blockage was calculated as 1-(signal treated ABP-UCHL1/signal DMSO ABP-UCHL1) × 100 %.

### Middle-down proteomics

UCHL1 (1 μg) was incubated with covalent fragment (typically 3–25 μM) for between 2 and 16 h. Protein–fragment reactions were diluted with an equal volume of 8 M urea/50 mM ammonium bicarbonate, treated with 100 ng endoproteinase AspN (Promega, Madison, WI) for ~15 min at 37C, and then quenched with 10 % formic acid. N-terminal and C-terminal fragments from UCHL1 were loaded on onto a self-packed column (5 cm 50R2 packed into 500 μm PEEK tubing) and eluted using an HPLC gradient (0–100 % B in 1 min, A = 0.2 M acetic acid, B = 0.2 M acetic acid in acetonitrile) and subjected to CID MS/MS on a 7600 Zeno-Tof mass spectrometer (AB-Sciex) with a spray voltage of 5.5 kV. The mass spectrometer acquired MS1 scans and targeted CID MS/MS scans for labeled peptides (CE typically 15–25 eV, unit resolution). Covalent modification of C52, C90, and C132 on the N-terminal fragment was determined by quantification of unmodified and modified y 16 3 + and y 90 12 + (<100 % at y 90 12 + assumed on C52). Labeling of C152, C201, and C220 on the C-terminal fragment was determined by quantification of unmodified and modified y 12 2 + , y 28 4 + , y 77 10 + ions. The three most abundant isotope peaks of each ion were summed for quantification (except for y 12 2 + where only two peaks were of significant intensity).

### UCHL1/UCHL3 mixed reaction assay

UCHL1 and UCHL3 (1 μg each) were mixed and diluted with PBS to a final concentration of 1 μM, reacted with indicated compounds for 2 h at room temperature, and analyzed by LC–MS. Stoichiometry of UCHL1 was assessed from the peak height of doubly labeled protein, as middle down MS experiments indicated the second labeling event occupied the catalytic cysteine.

### Spectral library construction

A DUB-specific spectral library was generated from several independent samples of ABPP-enriched DUBs (protocol below) using HEK293 cell extracts. Following trypsin digestion, the peptides were analyzed using an optimized data-independent acquisition method on a tims-TOF Flex2 instrument. The spectral library was generated in DIA-NN (1.8.2 beta 8) using a library-free approach. The following search parameters were used: MS1 accuracy: 15 ppm, MS2 accuracy: 10 ppm, fixed carbamidomethylation of cysteines (+57.02146), variable oxidation of methionines (+15.9949), variable modification of cysteines with the tryptic remnants of the ubiquitin vinyl ester and ubiquitin propargyl amide probes (+172.085, +112.064 respectively). N-terminus methionine excision was enabled along with unrestricted digestion C-terminal of arginine and lysine residues, allowing 2 missed cleavages. Additional parameters were specified as follows: minimum fragment m/z set to 200, maximum fragment m/z set to 1800, minimum peptide length set to 6, maximum peptide length set to 40, minimum precursor m/z set to 300, maximum precursor m/z set to 1800, minimum precursor charge set to 2 and maximum precursor charge set to 6. Library precursors were reannotated using a FASTA database of human sequences downloaded from UniProt on 2023-08-10 appended to common contaminants. Only spectral matches with a q-value <0.01 were retained.

### Activity-based protein profiling

Pellets of HEK293T cells were lysed with 50 mM Tris pH 8.0, 150 mM NaCl, 0.5 mM EDTA, 0.5 % NP-40, 10 % glycerol and the lysate was clarified by centrifugation (14,000 rpm for 15 min at 4 °C). Protein concentration was measured by BCA and aliquots of extract were treated with indicated compounds for 4 h at room temperature. An equal mixture of ubiquitin activity probes (ABP; Ub-PA/VME; 50 μM probe/mg protein; UbiQ, Amsterdam, Netherlands) was then added and allowed to react for 15 min at room temperature. Magnetic streptavidin beads (Cytiva, Marlborough, MA) were added to capture proteins bound by the ABP and washed with PBS/0.2 % SDS to reduce the level of non-specifically bound proteins. Enriched proteins were then eluted with hexafluoroisopropanol. Eluted proteins were digested on STRAP micro columns (Protifi, Long Island, NY) according to the manufacturer instructions. Peptides were loaded onto EVO tips (Odense, Denmark) according to the manufacturer instructions and analyzed with a 20-SPD method on an EVO Sep One (column = 75 μm I.D. packed with 15 cm 1.5 μm Dr. Maisch C18 [ESI Source Solutions, Woburn, MA] with integrated emitter tip [44]) coupled to a Bruker timsTOF Flex2 mass spectrometer operated in DIA mode. For each compound, triplicates of each treatment (0, 5, 10, and 25 μm) for 2 independent experiments were analyzed (n = 6). Data files were processed with DIA-NN version 1.8.2 beta 8 using a custom spectral library of DUBs (see ‘Spectral Library Construction’ above). Other DIA-NN search settings were the same as above, except that MS1 and MS2 mass accuracies were set to auto-inference. After filtering DIA-NN results for precursors with intensity >1000, differential abundance analysis was performed using MS-DAP [45], using default settings (https://github.com/ftwkoopmans/msdap) with filter_min_peptide_per_prot = 2, dea_qvalue_threshold =0.05, and diffdetect_min _peptides_observed = 3. Heat maps were generated with Python 3.12 and show values for blockage > 50 % and q-value <0.05 (msempire).

## Results

Fig. 1 highlights major hardware/software components along with user-input and performance criteria for our open source, medium-throughput covalent screening platform. We obtained libraries of commercial electrophilic compounds from Enamine (3200 compounds) and Chemdiv (1000 compounds), >70 % of which were selective for cysteine residues (Supplementary Fig. 5). We wrote a Python app (CreateScreenPools.py, Fig. 1 top, left) to distribute covalent fragments first by warhead (33 bins, Supplementary Table 3), and then into pools of ≤ five compounds with sufficient mass separation (~10 Da, accounting for leaving groups) to enable deconvolution of target-fragment binding on low-resolution mass spectrometers. We further annotated each compound entry in CreateScreenPools.py with its associated SMILES string to ensure that chemical structure is tracked and incorporated into the final screen report. For the screen reported herein, the pool plates comprised 855 pools across 3 × 384 well plates distributed as follows: 1) acrylamides and cyanoacrylamides, 2) chloroacetamides, chloropropylamides, and chloroketones, 3) other warheads (Supplementary Table 3). Next, we used a Beckman i7 liquid handler to dispense target protein across matching wells and dispense pool plate compounds. After 2 h, each reaction plate was quenched with formic acid and frozen until mass spectrometry analysis.

To achieve a primary screen throughput of at least 10,000 fragments per day, we assembled a gantry style autosampler with x-y actuators to position well-plates below a sampling needle mounted on the z-axis actuator. The syringe alternated delivery of samples from each well into one of two identical flow paths comprising a sample loop and reversed phase microcapillary column which are parallelized across multiple 2- and 10 position, multi-port valves. The terminal valve serves to direct column eluent to the mass spectrometer electrospray interface. Standard pressure liquid chromatography pumps provide solvent flow for sample loading and desalting as well as organic gradient for elution of protein-ligand conjugates from the reversed phase columns. We wrote RobotControl.py deployed on a Raspberry pi 3.0 to calibrate syringe position as a function of well-plate geometry (number and depth of wells), control sample pick-up and delivery, and trigger LC gradient and mass spectrometer acquisition via contact closure. Another Python script (SmpListWizard.py) was executed on the mass spectrometer instrument computer to automatically create file names based on output from CreateScreenPools.py and then use these to populate the sample acquisition queue. This platform configuration enabled interleaved sample injection, de-salting, and ballistic 24 s organic gradient delivery across parallel flow paths to achieve LC–MS acquisition of intact protein mass spectra in 37 s. per well, corresponding to 2335 injections (11,675 fragments) in 24 h. Finally, we wrote FragmentScreen.py to automate processing of native mass spectrometry data files to identify potential fragment binding. Results are provided in PowerPoint slides for manual inspection or figure creation as well as excel/csv to support programmatic integration with other structural, SAR, or chemi-informatic tools.

We first sought to assess the speed, reproducibility, and carryover of our autosampler mass spectrometry system. Towards this end we arrayed 3 purified proteins (cytochrome c, enolase, and UCHL1) across 192 wells, (64 wells each) of a 384-well plate, along with 192 PBS blanks. Each protein (25 ng/μL) was injected in a volume of 40 μL (1 μg protein) followed by injection from a blank well. Consistent with our design and timing estimates, completion of 384 injections required just under 4 h of analysis time. Fig. 2 (left) shows representative spectra for intact mass of each protein with violin plots (right) of summed peak intensity for each protein and blank injection. CVs for protein injections were <15 % with carryover <1 % in the blank injections. These results confirm the throughput, reproducibility, and low carryover of our open-source screening platform.

Having established baseline analytical performance for our screening platform we turned to our target of interest, ubiquitin c-terminal hydrolase L1 (UCHL1). UCHL1 is a small (~28 kDa) well-structured cysteine protease DUB comprising multiple alpha-helices and beta sheets, a catalytic triad, as well as five other cysteine residues (Fig. 3A). Although UCHL1 has potential oncogenic activity in multiple cancers, existing small molecule inhibitors show disparate performance. For example, early-generation UCHL1 inhibitors LDN57444 [46], LDN91946 [47] and Z-VAE(OMe)-fmk [48] are now recognized to lack cellular target engagement and/or exhibit poor selectivity which limits their utility as chemical probes. More recently, cyanamide [17,20–22,49] (primarily cyanopyrrolidine) and chloroacetohydrazide [19] inhibitors of UCHL1 have been described (see Table 1 for representative structures). While these compounds have been useful in some cell-based assays, none have progressed to in vivo studies potentially due to chemical or metabolic liabilities. Moreover, these compounds have not been uniformly tested for their off-target activity. These gaps motivated our interest to discover new chemical starting points for UCHL1.

Before initiating the library screen, we analyzed UCHL1 treated with DMSO (negative control) or the previously reported inhibitor SB-1-F22 [17] (positive control). From this pilot screen we determined the Z’-factor to be 0.75, indicating that our platform can reliably identify UCHL1 covalent hit-fragments [50]. For the library screen, we prepared reaction plates as described above, comprising 855 fragment pools, each incubated in a 12.5-fold molar excess (12.5 μM) with 1 μg of UCHL1 for 2 h at room temperature. Reactions were quenched with 1 % formic acid and analyzed directly from each reaction plate as described above using RobotControl.py and SmpListWizard.py.

Native mass spectrometry data files (.RAW) were directly processed using Fragment Screening.py that leverages the multiplierz toolkit [42] to read raw mass spectrometry data files. For each injection the average mass spectrum was extracted from the primary LC elution peak and deconvoluted with Unidec [41] to yield intact mass of UCHL1 along with signals for fragment-labeled and potential multi-labeled UCHL1. The script also provides an estimate of the binding stoichiometry, allowing prioritization of fragments. As illustrated in Fig. 3B, in the primary screen of pooled fragments we identified 41 compounds with binding stoichiometry ≥35 % (see Supplementary Table 4). Most ‘hit’ fragments were cyanoacrylamides (63 %), followed by chloroacetamides (21 %), a few chloroketones, and one acrylamide. Fig. 3C and D show deconvoluted spectra output by Fragmentscreening.py. The colored vertical lines indicate unlabeled UCHL1 along with calculated masses for UCHL1 labeled with each fragment in the pool. Peaks at higher masses suggest possible multi-labeling by one or more of the fragments. These spectra are packaged into PowerPoint slides, providing a convenient way to visually assess the credibility of top hits from the Excel report.

We validated hit fragments by incubating individual compounds at a reduced 6.25-fold molar excess (6.25 μM) with UCHL1. Consistent with lower compound concentration we set a minimum threshold of 15 % binding stoichiometry. Indeed, 39 of 41 fragments passed this step, corresponding to a validation rate >95 % for the primary screen. Moreover, at the reduced concentration, 11 fragments exhibited predominantly mono-labeling. For the remining 28 hits, we performed serial dilutions to identify 16 fragments which exhibited mono-labeling at ~3 μM. In total, these secondary screens validated a set of 27 hit-fragments suitable for subsequent characterization across orthogonal assays.

To test for inhibitory activity, we employed ubiquitin rhodamine 110 as a substrate in a kinetic assay (Fig. 4A) [51,52]. Of the 27 compounds tested, six inhibited UCHL1 with IC50 values <25 μM (n = 4) and three at <10 μM (n = 4). Interestingly, Z203045204 and Z56871617 (IC50 3.7 and 14 μM), contain a benzothiazole adjacent to the electrophile, which may mediate reversible interactions proximal to the catalytic triad to position the warhead for covalent modification of the catalytic cysteine (C90). The remaining fragments, including all the cyanoacrylamides, exhibited no inhibitory activity (IC50 values >25 μM), or did not achieve maximum inhibition at the highest dose (Supplementary Table 5) and were removed from further consideration. To evaluate the inhibitory mechanism-of-action, we first used a ubiquitin activity-based probe (Ub-ABP) with purified UCHL1 to assess target engagement by SDS-PAGE for each hit compound (Fig. 4B). We observed dose dependent blocking of ABP binding (>50 % at 50 μM) for 5 validated hit-fragments, including benzothiazole core compounds Z203045204 and Z56871617 (Fig. 4C, full gels available in Supplementary Data 1). To confirm site(s) of fragment binding and stoichiometry, we utilized middle down mass spectrometry. We first established limited digestion conditions with the endoprotease Asp-N that yielded two UCHL1 peptides—an N-terminal 16.3 kDa peptide containing C52, C90 (catalytic cys), and C132 and an 8.9 kDa C-terminal peptide containing C152, C201, and C220 (Fig. 4D). Subsequent collision induced dissociation on a quadrupole time-of-flight mass spectrometer was used to quantify covalent labeling at each cysteine residue on the two UCHL1 peptides after a 2 h treatment with compound. Consistent with the biochemical assays, we found that all 5 fragments covalently modified the UCHL1 catalytic cysteine residue C90 (Fig. 4E). Interestingly, they also labeled C152, the “bridge” or “cross-over” cysteine contained in a nearby disordered loop. This cysteine has been proposed to serve as a redox sensor [53] to protect the catalytic residue. To further explore fragment reactivities with C90 and C152, Z203045204 and Z56871617 were reacted at a lower concentration (3 μM) at short (2 h) and long (16 h) time points. C152 was modified first (2 h) and the catalytic residue (C90) was labeled after further incubation (16 h, Fig. 4F).

To examine selectivity of these compounds toward other UCHL family members, we reacted each of the 5 validated fragments with an equimolar mixture of UCHL-1 and UCHL-3 and evaluated the stoichiometry of labeling (Fig. 5A). The two chloroacetamide compounds—Z203045204 and Z56871617, exhibited strong selectivity for UCHL1. In fact, these compounds showed no reaction with UCHL3 at concentrations up to 50 μM. In contrast, the remaining 3 chloroketone compounds showed high levels of reactivity to both DUBs. Encouraged by the in vitro binding profiles of Z203045204 and Z56871617, we turned to activity-based protein profiling (ABPP) with mass spectrometry to assess the binding selectivity of both compounds against endogenous DUBs in a near-physiological context. Z56871617 showed no activity against any of the 57 DUBs reproducibly quantified at concentrations up to 25 μM (data not shown), while Z203045204 displaced the Ub-ABP (>50 %) from UCHL1 in a dose-dependent manner at 10 and 25 μM. Notably, Z203045204 was not active against sub-family members UCHL3 or UCHL5, and exhibited binding to BAP1, as well as USP5, USP8, and USP37/38, only at the highest concentration. Collectively, these results demonstrate a favorable selectivity profile for electrophilic fragment Z203045204 and suggest that it may serve as a useful starting point for future chemical optimization towards a covalent UCHL1 inhibitor.

## Discussion

Covalent inhibitors have often been developed by structure-guided elaboration of an existing reversible ligand with an electrophilic warhead (‘ligand-first’) [54–56]. More recently, an ‘electrophile-first’ strategy, whereby covalent fragment libraries are screened to identify an initial binder, followed by chemical elaboration to build selectivity, has come to the fore [25,28,57]. Mass spectrometry is particularly well-suited for characterization of covalent compound-protein adduct [16,26,58]. The Agilent Rapid Fire SPE-MS platform [59] is well-established as a ‘go-to’ system for high-throughput LC–MS screening applications, with inject-to-inject time of ~15 s per sample. Recently, higher throughput systems based on acoustic ejection [60] and IR-MALDESI [61] have also been reported. However, in contrast to typical diversity libraries, electrophilic fragment collections span broad chemical space with a comparatively modest number of compounds. As a result, target-based screens with covalent fragment libraries can be productively executed with medium-throughput approaches. Given these criteria we saw an opportunity to leverage open hardware principles [38–40,62–64] to assemble a fit-for-purpose mass spectrometry-based platform for covalent fragment screening that would reduce costs while increasing design, operational, and data analysis transparency. Towards this goal we used a combination of readily available and economical extruded aluminum and 3D printed construction elements, general-use precision motorized components, commodity microcontroller boards, and raspberry Pi microcomputers, to build a parallelized sample injection system to support rapid analysis (<40 s/sample) of intact protein-ligand conjugates by LC–MS. As described herein our system does rely on a commercial mass spectrometer and HPLC pumps; however, we intentionally chose systems that are unequivocally on the low end of the performance (and therefore cost) scale by current standards in chemoproteomics. We further provide software tools to facilitate pooling of library compounds, generation and management of target-compound reactions and filenames for intact protein mass spectrometry analysis, as well as automated processing of screening data. Consistent with open hardware and software principles, we provide (through the supplementary materials) extensive and standardized hardware design and assembly documentation. This information includes openSCAD files for 3D printed components, detailed parts list, build instructions, and operation manual. We also provide Python and other code specific for the screening platform as well as links to our and others’ open source software tools that support analysis of fragment screening data. Importantly, results are output in human- and machine-readable formats and include information for compound structures. In this way our screening data is immediately interoperable with other chemi-informatics analysis tools like DataWarrior [65] or RDKit [66].

Open hardware design seeks to improve design and operational transparency while reducing the costs associated with advanced scientific instruments and workflows. These are conceptually laudable goals and can help democratize access to what are otherwise proprietary and expensive technologies. However, in practice widespread adoption of this paradigm requires that practitioners can leverage these benefits to achieve actionable results comparable to purpose-built commercial platforms. With a throughput of ~10,000 compounds per day, our platform readily supports target-based screens against electrophilic fragment libraries. Indeed, covalent fragment screens performed on the commercial [59] and research [60,61] platforms noted above are also in the range of 3000–10,000 covalent compounds. The number of fragments notwithstanding, one potential advantage of the higher throughput offered by these recently reported systems is the ability to analyze compounds individually and hence complete the primary screen in approximately the same time as a pooled format screen. As a powerful proof-of-performance we executed a covalent fragment screen against UCHL1, a DUB that has been nominated as a therapeutic target in neurodegenerative disease and cancer. Primary and secondary screens performed on our open hardware platform yielded 27 UCHL1 covalent binders. Of these, we validated 5 hits that inhibited enzyme activity (IC50 <25 μM), blocked the binding of a Ubiquitin-ABP (≥50 %), and covalently modified the catalytic cysteine (C90). Two of these compounds (Z203045204 and Z56871617) exhibited no binding in in vitro experiments with the closely related family member UCHL3 at concentrations up to 50 μM. And in ABPP experiments performed in cell extracts, only Z203045204 blocked binding of the ubiquitin probe to UCHL1 and otherwise showed excellent selectivity for a primary screening hit across 57 endogenous DUBs. Indeed, our success in prosecuting hits from the primary screen through a series of orthogonal validation assays to nominate Z203045204 as a promising starting point for a UCHL1 inhibitor credentials the fit-for-purpose performance of our open hardware platform. Moreover, our ability to validate cyanoacrylamide compounds as primary hits demonstrates that our platform is generally suitable for screening reversible-covalent fragments [67]. Beyond validation of UCHL1 binding in the primary screen, we note that none of the cyanoacrylamide hit compounds showed evidence of inhibitory activity by the Ub-Rho or target engagement biochemical assays. While beyond the scope of this report, it will be interesting in future studies to explore whether the cysteine(s) modified by these reversible-covalent compounds reside in novel pockets which could be leveraged for development of recruiter or other novel mechanism-of-action modalities.

The deubiquitinating enzymes (DUBs) comprise a family of approximately 100 structurally and functionally related enzymes that catalyze the cleavage of ubiquitin and ubiquitin-like (UBL) post-translational marks from substrate proteins. As key members of the ubiquitinproteasome system (UPS), DUBs are functionally involved in numerous cellular processes1. Moreover, DUBs have been linked to human cancer and neurodegenerative disease2, suggesting that DUB inhibitors could have a signiﬁcant therapeutic impact. However, efforts to demonstrate the clinical beneﬁt of DUB inhibition have been hampered by the poor selectivity of early compounds, as well as a limited understanding of DUB biology, especially the scope of unique and shared substrates across the family of DUB enzymes. A dedicated platform to develop selective DUB inhibitors would provide tool compounds (chemical

probes) and drug discovery leads to advance both basic and translational understanding of this large protein family. The majority of the annotated DUBs are cysteine proteases, which are further classiﬁed into six subfamilies based on sequence homology2. A combination of shared and unique structural features surrounding the catalytic site, along with diversity in primary sequence suggest that cysteine protease DUBs can be selectively targeted with small molecule inhibitors. Early generation DUB inhibitors have been found in retrospect to be multitargeted3,4. Results A DUB-focused library × library screening platform Our rationally designed library was inspired by diverse DUB inhibitor chemotypes. (Fig. 1a) These include a selective USP7 inhibitor, XL177A developed in our lab20, N-cyanopyrrolidines including SB1-F-22 identiﬁed in a patent from Mission Therapeutics and validated in-house to modify the active site cysteine of UCHL121–23 (Supplementary Fig. 1), and AV12 (referred to as 1 in the reporting manuscript) which binds multiple DUBs24. We analyzed DUB-ligand/-ubiquitin co-structures25–28

(Fig. 1b) to identify regions around the catalytic site that may favor compound interaction, as well as possible determinants of selectivity. We then implemented a combinatorial assembly of noncovalent building blocks, linkers, and electrophilic warheads. The noncovalent building blocks incorporated a variety of aromatic and heterocycle moieties to harness interactions with blocking loops 1 and 2 in the leucine-binding pocket S427,28. The linkers were designed to mimic the C-terminal residues of ubiquitin (GG) and traverse a narrow channel leading up to the catalytic cysteine (Fig. 1b)25. To capitalize on structural and sequence variation in this channel across DUBs, we diversi- ﬁed length, ﬂexibility, and presentation of hydrogen bond donor/ acceptor groups in the linker. We anticipated that interactions between each chemical component and the catalytic diad/triad as well as less-conserved, neighboring regions on each DUB would contribute to overall binding potency and selectivity. We synthesized most library compounds with a reactive component comprising a ring system elaborated with an electrophile. This design was inspired by our chemotypes and differentiates our library from general electrophile collections which have been largely unsuccessful in yielding DUB ligands. The reactive groups span four general categories: cyano, α,β-unsaturated amide/sulfonamide,

chloroacetamide and halogenated aromatics. We diversiﬁed within each category with respect to electrophilic functionality as well as pendant ring system (Supplementary Data 1, Synthetic procedures provided in Supplementary Methods). Finally, the library also included a small number (<10) of putatively covalent DUB inhibitors. We chose activity-based protein proﬁling (ABPP) coupled with quantitative mass spectrometry as the primary screen platform (Fig. 1c, Supplementary Fig. 2). In general, DUB ABPs consist of ubiquitin protein to confer DUB speciﬁcity, an C-terminal electrophile to form a covalent attachment to the DUB catalytic cysteine residue, and an afﬁnity handle at the N-terminus to enable DUB enrichment by capture on streptavidin beads (Supplementary Fig. 2a)29. In the experiments in this manuscript, we utilize a 1:1 combination of biotin- Ub-VME and biotin-Ub-PA (Supplementary Fig. 2a). To maximize DUB coverage as well as compound throughput and peptide detection, we used a combination of DUB ABPs along with isobaric TMT multiplexed reagents and our true nanoﬂow LC columns with integrated electrospray emitters30,31. While not typically used at this early stage of inhibitor development, we reasoned that performing this competitive binding assay in a library × library format would accelerate progress on two fronts. First, the assay format maximizes our ability to identify hits against a large number of DUBs in their endogenous, native environment. Second, the integration of ABPP results across our library provides valuable insight for DUB family structure-activity relationships. These SAR data can simultaneously inform medicinal chemistry optimization of hits as well as guide design of new libraries. We tested our chemoproteomic ABPP assay using foundation chemotypes (Fig. 1a) as well as previously characterized multitargeted DUB inhibitors PR-619 and HBX411083. These validation data spanned 54 cellular DUBs, which represents a signiﬁcant advance in coverage compared with recent reports and recapitulated the DUB binding proﬁles expected for our selective chemotypes as well as the promiscuous covalent compounds (Fig. 1d, e)6,32.

Primary screen and hit identiﬁcation We next initiated the primary screen of our library, comprising 178 DUB-focused compounds each incubated at a single concentration of 50 µM in cellular protein extracts. We analyzed the entire library across 25 multiplexed chemoproteomic ABPP acquisitions. We ﬁrst assessed the platform by analyzing ABPP assay performance and then characterizing primary hits against the DUB family. In total, we detected 65 distinct DUBs, representing 75% of the cysteine protease DUB enzymes expressed in HEK293 cells as reported in the Human Protein Atlas33. Consistent with our platform validation data, we detected on average 58 DUBs per ABPP run (Supplementary Fig. 3b). Importantly, combinatorial sampling of data across all multiplexed acquisitions indicated that the number of DUBs reproducibly detected stabilized at 49, with 56 DUBs detected in >80% of runs (Fig. 2a). Taken together, results from our analytical validation and primary screen suggest that our DUB-ABPP platform is well-suited for identiﬁcation of hits against individual DUBs while also providing SAR data across the target class. To focus our analysis on the most promising compounds we deﬁned a ‘hit compound’ as a compound that blocked ≥50% of ABP labeling for at least a single DUB. More than 60% of library compounds were active, suggesting good ﬁdelity between our chemical diversiﬁ- cation strategy and binding activity against the target class. Consistent with ﬁrst-generation libraries designed for other enzyme classes34,35, the number of DUBs targeted by each compound varied broadly (Fig. 2b). Impressively, 60 of the compounds (just over 50% of all hits) displayed excellent selectivity proﬁles, targeting only 1-3 DUBs. The remaining hit compounds were split among those targeting 4-6 or 6+ DUBs. Other ubiquitin interacting enzymes (e.g. E1, E2, E3 enzymes) were not competitively bound by the library compounds, supporting potential speciﬁcity for DUBs (Supplementary Fig. 3a) and further validating our strategy for library design. Taken together these results highlight the power of quantitative ABPP as a primary screen to simultaneously identify hit-compounds and discern SAR trends. Consistent with our multi-site diversiﬁcation strategy, we observed that distinct regions of DUB active sites (catalytic and nearby residues, narrow channel leading to the active site, the blocking loops and the P4 pocket) all contribute to selectivity.

Orthogonal hit validation Our primary ABPP screen yielded selective hit-compounds for 23 DUBs, spanning 4 DUB families (MJD, USP, UCH, OTU). Among these, we prioritized compounds targeting 9 different DUBs (UCHL1, UCHL3, USP16, USP27X, USP28, USP30, USP48, JOSD1 and VCPIP1), representing four subfamilies, for validation studies. Compound selection was based on strength of competitive binding along with structural and target diversity. We ﬁrst re-tested all prioritized hit-compounds in a 3-point dose–response implementation of our ABPP MS assay (Fig. 4a, Supplementary Fig. 3c). In addition, we conﬁrmed competitive ABP-compound binding by western blotting ﬁrst in cell lysate (Fig. 4b, Supplementary Fig. 4, Supplementary Data 3), then in live cells (Supplementary Fig. 5). Cell viability was unaltered during 24-h compound treatments at 0.25x-4x biochemical IC50 for 5 out of 6 compounds selected, each targeting a different DUB (Supplementary Fig. 5). We next biochemically validated inhibition of DUB activity. The potencies

of hit compounds varied from sub-micromolar to double-digit micromolar, on par with typical hits from a high-throughput screen (Fig. 4b, Supplementary Tables 2, 3). We next combined datadependent and targeted LC-MS/MS along with intact protein mass spectrometry to conﬁrm 1:1 ligand binding and covalent modiﬁcation of the catalytic cysteine for UCHL1, UCHL3, USP7, USP48, USP28, and VCPIP1 ligands (Supplementary Fig. 6, Supplementary Table 4). Overall, we observed good cell permeability, minimal toxicity, high con- ﬁrmation rates and excellent agreement for assays spanning compound binding in both live cell and lysates, mechanism of action, and enzyme inhibition for library hits targeting UCHL1, UCHL3, USP28, USP48 and VCPIP1 (Fig. 4b). N-cyanopyrrolidines were strongly represented among hit-compounds, including F-70 which selectively bound UCHL1 with 400nM potency, as previously reported21,36. We synthesized a desthiobiotinylated analog (dtb-F-70) and co-incubated it with the native compound in cell extracts followed by multiplexed chemoproteomic analysis. These data conﬁrmed UCHL1 as one of only 6 competitively bound targets throughout the proteome (Fig. 4c, Supplementary Data 4). Interestingly, two off-target enzymes (DESI-2 and ATG4B) were recently reported to deconjugate UBL marks, suggesting that N-cyanopyrrolidines may represent a privileged scaffold for UB- and UBL-targeted proteases37,38.

Towards this end, we treated cellular protein extracts with either vehicle (DMSO), 50 µM WH-9943-103C, or 50 µM XL177A (negative control for VCPIP1 covalent binding) followed by trypsin digest, TMT stable isotope labeling, and biochemical enrichment of cysteine-containing peptides. We performed quantitative, multiplexed chemoproteomic cysteine proﬁling using both targeted and datadependent MS/MS acquisition strategies to characterize the covalent binding of WH-9943-103C on VCPIP1 as well as across the broader set of cysteine residues across proteome, respectively (Supplementary Fig. 7, Supplementary Data 5)39. In contrast we took a ‘next-generation’ target-class approach to DUB inhibitor development. We eschew agnostic chemical diversity and instead leveraged a structure-guided approach to design a modestsized library purposely diversiﬁed around electrophile and pendant ring system, as well as the linker to build selectivity through multiple sites of DUB-small molecule engagement. As highlighted throughout this report, our use of activity-based protein proﬁling against endogenous DUBs enabled us to simultaneously deconvolute hits as well as DUB-family SAR in a high-content primary screen. The chemical, biochemical, and chemoproteomic methods we employed are scalable and accessible in a wide range of research environments. In this way our platform democratizes a powerful alternative to the current trend towards massive libraries coupled with ultra-high throughput screening technology. Efforts in sequencing, genomics, and other systematic molecular analyses continue to highlight DUBs as key nodes in the functional proteome, as well as potential disease vulnerabilities41. However, a lack of potent and selective chemical probes represents a signiﬁcant hurdle in interrogating DUB biology or validating their potential as drug targets. In this respect our results represent a watershed in de-risking DUB inhibitor development. Our combinatorial library diversiﬁcation strategy yielded selective hits for 23 DUBs spanning 4 DUB families, including examples outside the precedented range of targeted DUBs with foundational chemotypes and for which there are no existing ligands. In fact, for some of the most understudied DUBs our results may motivate development of assays as well as antibodies and other reagents to support comprehensive functional studies. We credit the high hit rate and broad DUB coverage to the success of our rational design strategy; tailoring the screening library to structural elements of the DUB active site, then diversifying against multiple points of targetcompound interactions identiﬁed in existing inhibitor/DUB costructures. Additionally, our results provide further evidence that covalent mechanism of action represents a promising path for the development of new selective DUB inhibitors. Our high-content primary screen in which we proﬁled 178 compounds against 56 DUBs revealed multi-parameter SAR trends which will accelerate future studies. As a powerful example, we leveraged these insights to rapidly optimize a hit for the understudied DUB, VCPIP1, into a potent and selective probe. Importantly, our selective hit-compounds span well-studied DUBs such as UCHL1 as well as some of the most understudied DUBs including USP43, USP53 and OTUD7A. Given the family wide hit diversity, our library provides a multitude of promising chemical starting points and a direct path to tool compounds that can be used to decipher DUB function, ubiquitin substrates, and biochemical pathways. In this way our next-gen target class approach provides a road map for inhibitor development against other understudied proteins or gene-families.

The mass spectrometer collected ion mobility MS spectra over a mass range of m/z 100–1700 and 1/k0 of 0.6 to 1.6, and then performed 10 cycles of PASEF MS/MS with a target intensity of 14.5k and a threshold of 1750. The experiment targeting the VCPIP1 endogenous and synthetic peptides was performed using PRM-LIVE39

(+3 to +5 charge states for each peptide, ±0.025 V s/cm2, isolation width 0.7 Da, tims stepping enabled). In this experiment, peptides were loaded directly on the analytical column and eluted with an LC gradient (2–17% B in 90 min, 17–25% B in 45 min, 25–37% B in 30 min, 37–80% B in 22.5 min, 80–95% B in 1.5 min; A = water with 0.1% formic acid, B = acetonitrile with 0.1% formic acid; spray voltage = 1600 V). The search parameters used trypsin as the protease with 2 missed cleavages allowed, precursor mass tolerance of 20 ppm, and product ion tolerance of 0.05 Da. Modiﬁcations included variable methionine oxidation, ﬁxed cysteine carbamidomethylation, and ﬁxed lysine and N-terminal TMT labeling. A false discovery rate of 1% was used as a cutoff for peptide identiﬁcation. Data were further processed using in-house scripts to extract TMT reporter ion intensities for each PSM. For the PRM run, PSMs spanning the full-width-half-max of the VCPIP1 peptide elution proﬁle were combined and reporter intensities were compared to determine a relative fold-change between the control (DMSO) and treatment (WH- 9943-103C) conditions. Search results for DDA PASEF MS/MS analysis from the other peptide fractions were combined for statistical analysis. We excluded PSMs with a missing value in any of the TMT reporter channels. The remaining PSMs were corrected for TMT isotopic impurities. In cases where multiple spectra matched to the same combination of sequence, modiﬁcation, and charge state, we selected the PSM with the highest summed intensity across the two DMSO control channels (TMT126 and TMT129). Impurity-corrected reporter intensities less than 0 were replaced with an intensity value of 12, which was empirically determined to be the ~3 times the noise level in the m/z region of the TMT reporters. Next, intensity values were median normalized across channels. Pairs of median intensity values for the three replicate channels (TMT126-TMT129, TMT127-TMT130 and TMT128- TMT131) were used as input for a maximum likelihood estimation of parameters to derive an intensity-dependent error model and p-values for DMSO:inhibitor-treated ratio50. In vitro inflammation and toxicity assessment of pre‑ and post‑incinerated organomodified nanoclays to macrophages using high‑throughput screening approaches

Abstract Background  Organomodified nanoclays (ONC), two-dimensional montmorillonite with organic coatings, are increasingly used to improve nanocomposite properties. However, little is known about pulmonary health risks along the nanoclay life cycle even with increased evidence of airborne particulate exposures in occupational environments. Recently, oropharyngeal aspiration exposure to pre- and post-incinerated ONC in mice caused low grade, persistent lung inflammation with a pro-fibrotic signaling response with unknown mode(s) of action. We hypothesized that the organic coating presence and incineration status of nanoclays determine the inflammatory cytokine secretary profile and cytotoxic response of macrophages. To test this hypothesis differentiated human macrophages (THP-1) were acutely exposed (0–20 µg/cm2) to pristine, uncoated nanoclay (CloisNa), an ONC (Clois30B), their incinerated byproducts (I-CloisNa and I-Clois30B), and crystalline silica (CS) followed by cytotoxicity and inflammatory endpoints. Macrophages were co-exposed to lipopolysaccharide (LPS) or LPS-free medium to assess the role of priming the NF-κB pathway in macrophage response to nanoclay treatment. Data were compared to inflammatory responses in male C57Bl/6J mice following 30 and 300 µg/mouse aspiration exposure to the same particles. Results  In LPS-free media, CloisNa exposure caused mitochondrial depolarization while Clois30B exposure caused reduced macrophage viability, greater cytotoxicity, and significant damage-associated molecular patterns (IL-1α and ATP) release compared to CloisNa and unexposed controls. LPS priming with low CloisNa doses caused elevated cathepsin B/Caspage-1/IL-1β release while higher doses resulted in apoptosis. Clois30B exposure caused dosedependent THP-1 cell pyroptosis evidenced by Cathepsin B and IL-1β release and Gasdermin D cleavage. Incineration ablated the cytotoxic and inflammatory effects of Clois30B while I-CloisNa still retained some mild inflammatory potential. Comparative analyses suggested that in vitro macrophage cell viability, inflammasome endpoints, and proinflammatory cytokine profiles significantly correlated to mouse bronchioalveolar lavage inflammation metrics including inflammatory cell recruitment. Conclusions  Presence of organic coating and incineration status influenced inflammatory and cytotoxic responses following exposure to human macrophages. Background Research and development efforts of nanoclay-enabled technologies have steadily increased due to their use in advanced manufacturing of plastic nanocomposites [1– 3]. Little is known, however, whether nanoclay exposure poses an occupational health risk across its lifecycle with known high exposure levels (up to 39.2 mg/m3) [4–10]. Furthermore, in vitro nanoclay toxicity studies have been mostly restricted to epithelial cell responses with little effort to evaluate immune cell responses and immune system key events that lead to potential disease. There is a clear emerging need to further understand toxicological implications of nanoclay-enabled technologies across their life cycle to thus responsibly develop and implement safe nanoclay-based applications [6, 9]. One of the most popular nanoclays in advanced manufacturing, two dimensional (2D) smectite nanoclays (e.g. montmorillonite), possess a 2:1 phyllosilicate structure of an octahedral aluminum oxide sheet bounded by two tetrahedral silica oxide sheets on each side resulting in dimensions of 1 nm thick and hundreds of nm in length and width. Natural montmorillonite exists in a stacked mineral platelet morphology with hydrophilic properties. Addition of organic modifier coatings, such as quaternary ammonium tallow compounds (QACs), are used to improve nanoclay dispersion, rheology, barrier function, and thermal properties in composite materials [3, 11, 12]. Increased concern associated with ONC inhalation exposure in occupational settings along its lifecycle has driven pulmonary toxicity investigations. Inhalation of montmorillonite in miners resulted in a ‘silicosis-like’ lung pathology, most likely due to surface silica group reaction with lung tissue commonly associated with crystalline silica exposure [13, 14]. Addition of QAC coatings carries cell membrane and cytotoxicity hazards [15]. To address this, our group’s previous work conducted thorough physicochemical characterization on a library of pre- and post-incinerated nanoclays. Cloisite Na, a pristine, uncoated montmorillonite possesses single and stacked platelet morphology with a silicate (Si–O– Si) and aluminate (Al–OH–Al) surface chemistry. Its organic coating derivative, Cloisite 30B, possesses similar characteristics but with an additional methyl, tallow,

bis-2-hydroxyethyl, quaternary ammonium coating. Incineration of these two nanoclays resulted in I-CloisNa and I-Clois30B that possessed deformations of the OH linked to ­Al3− and ­Mg2− and increased presence of Al–O group. In addition, I-CloisNa still possessed Si–O–Si surface chemistry and a smooth surface consistent with amorphous silica. I-Clois30B surface chemistry analysis showed complete disappearance of the quaternary ammonium tallow coating with a heterogenous surface containing smooth amorphous, porous, or fused stacked platelet morphology suggesting that the presence of the organic coating caused partial retention of platelet structure [16, 17]. Comparative in vitro studies of pre-versus post-incinerated ­Cloisite® and ­Nanomer® ONCs largely reported that toxicity was influenced by the presence and type of the organic modifier, as well as incineration status in bronchial and small airway epithelial cell models [16, 18– 20]. Uncoated nanoclays and ONCs caused monolayer integrity loss and apoptosis with different dose response curves, suggesting different potency or modes of action. ONC exposure caused enhanced particle uptake, inconsistent changes in reactive oxygen species (ROS), mitochondrial degeneration, and increased genotoxicity (i.e., micronuclei and DNA breakage) [15, 21–23]. Conversely, incinerated nanoclays produced minimal effects [16, 18– 20]. Our group’s in vivo pulmonary toxicity assessment of pre- and post-incinerated Cloisite® nanoclays [17], reported that ONC (Cloisite® 30B) exposure resulted in a low grade, delayed inflammatory response, consisting of increased macrophage and neutrophil infiltrations, elevated damage markers, and elevated pro-fibrotic cytokines at day 28. Conversely, Cloisite® ­Na+ caused a robust inflammatory response with the same profibrotic signature as the ONC-exposed animals. Incinerated Cloisite® ­Na+ elicited a transient inflammatory response while incinerated Cloisite® 30B produced a chronic inflammatory response, similar to aged crystalline silica (CS) [24]. Recent studies by Di Ianni et al. [25] reported that presence of QAC coating on bentonite decreased toxicity in exposed mouse lung; however, the same ONC caused potent in vitro epithelial and macrophage toxicity [26] which aligns with our assessments. Collectively, it

Collectively, pre-incinerated nanoclay displayed interaction with macrophage membrane components (molecular initiating event), increased proinflammatory mediators, and increased inflammatory cell recruitment (two key events) in the lung fibrosis adverse outcome pathway. remains unclear what role pulmonary macrophages play in eliciting these observed in vivo effects. Very few studies on nanoclay exposure impacts to the immune system and chronic inflammation have been conducted but are critical since these responses to particle deposition typically drive lung pathology [27, 28]. At present, no thorough evaluation exists of how nanoclay exposure impacts lung macrophage cellular and inflammatory responses which can promote pulmonary disease. Defining lung macrophage and other major target cell’s response to ONC exposure would identify those key events in an adverse outcome pathway (AOP) framework to improve screening strategies and inform risk assessment [29]. Furthermore, correlating in  vitro response to in  vivo metrics across particle types and characteristics can assist in placing in  vitro models’ screening role in an integrated testing framework. A recent review identified the need for systematic in vitro/in vivo extrapolation studies, identification of immunomodulatory biomarkers, and characterization of changes in toxic effect over the nanoclay lifecycle [15]. Past attempts at using in  vitro models to predict in vivo effect following inhalation particle exposures has resulted in marginal success complicated by non-standardized test methods, particle kinetics, dosimetry, and differences in clearance mechanisms; however, recent improvements have occurred with use of the AOP paradigm [30–32]. Traditionally, in vitro studies with ultrafine particles to assess macrophage inflammatory and toxicity responses used LPS-primed macrophages [33]. Co-stimulation of macrophages with LPS allowed for priming of the inflammasome via NF-κB activation to evaluate the potential role of the NLRP3 inflammasome in driving inflammatory and toxicity response [28, 34]. Furthermore, it simulates a relevant occupational exposure (typically containing microbes and endotoxin) and mimics other priming signals (e.g. TNF) from other exposed cells [28]. However, a majority of lung particle exposures with animal models are typically conducted using sterile particle preparations under relatively sterile laboratory conditions [35, 36]. The absence of LPS allows for comparison of particle-induced inflammatory response across relatively sterile in  vitro versus in  vivo particle exposures and can assess whether a particle can activate the inflammasome in the absence of LPS. There is an inherent lack of in  vitro studies that performed direct comparisons between LPS- and non-LPS stimulated macrophages and how that compares to the in vivo animal model response. To address these issues, we conducted a study to investigate acute toxicity responses, several key events (KE) in the proposed ‘substance interaction with the pulmonary resident cell membrane components leading to pulmonary fibrosis’ AOP #173 [37], and potential underlying

mechanisms for lung macrophages following occupationally expected exposure levels to pre- and post-incinerated organomodified nanoclay. The objectives were to (1) assess how differences in coating and incineration status determines differentiated macrophage response, and (2) correlate in  vitro macrophage endpoints to in  vivo responses. We hypothesized that the organic coating presence and incineration status of nanoclays determine the inflammatory cytokine secretary profile and cytotoxic response of macrophages. Herein, we report on particle characterization and macrophage toxicity and inflammatory responses to help further understand toxic effects observed in vivo.

Methods Particle preparation and characterization To screen and evaluate coating and incineration effects on nanoclays’ potential for lung cell in vitro adverse outcomes, pristine (Cloisite® Na + ; CloisNa) and an organomodified nanoclay (Cloisite® 30B; Clois30B) were purchased from Southern Clay Products (Gonzalez, TX). To model particles generated during end-of-life municipal incineration, both CloisNa and Clois30B were subjected to incineration during thermogravimetric analysis (900 °C for 100 min) and collected as incinerated nanoclays I-CloisNa and I-Clois30B as previously described [16]. Based on dry particle diameter and chemistry, heat inactivated crystalline silica (CS; Min-U-Sil 5; US Silica; Berkeley Springs, WV) was used as a benchmark particle for all studies. Non-freshly fractured (i.e. aged) Min-U-Sil 5 particle samples were dry heated at 180 °C for several hours to remove endotoxin and held at room temperature until used. Aged CS loses most of its silicon and siloxyl radicals compared to freshly fractured silica, but still retains silica structure and some inflammatory potential similar to pyrogenic silica [14, 24, 38]. All particle samples were UV sterilized and fully characterized for water and organic modifier content, surface chemistry, particle morphology, and elemental analysis by thermal gravimetric analysis, Fourier transform infrared spectroscopy, field emission scanning electron microscopy, and energy-dispersive x-ray spectroscopy, respectively, in previous publications [16, 17]. Stock particle suspensions (3 to 5 ml at 1 mg/mL) were made by adding sterile MilliQ water to known particle mass in sterile glass test tubes. Discrete sonication was used to disperse stock particle suspensions. Briefly, particle suspensions were lightly vortexed and sonicated three separate times (200.4 J/ml per run) with a cup horn (Sonics VibraCell VCX-750; Newton, CT) at 40% intensity immersed in cold water with a one-minute rest between sonications. This achieved a total critical sonication energy ­(DSEcr = 601.2  J/ml) needed to reach relatively

Statistical analyses Dose–response curves were modeled and fitted using the “drc” package [52] using the R v. 3.6.1 statistical program (R Foundation for Statistical Computing, Vienna, Austria). The effective dose to cause a 50% reduction in the measured response ­(ED50) compared to the control and associated estimate standard deviation were derived from fitted models using the “drc” package. ­ED50 values that exceeded the highest dose test (20 μg/cm2) were designated as > 20  μg/cm2. Statistical comparisons between modeled ­ED50 were performed via a two-sample t test. Where appropriate, defined ­ED50 value comparisons against particle effective doses designated as > 20  μg/ cm2 were performed using a one-sample t-test, wherein the null value was set to 20. Differences in particle characteristics in media were determined by one-way analysis of variance (ANOVA). To determine differences in macrophage responses among treatment groups, 2-way ANOVAs were conducted. All data were evaluated for variance homoscedasticity and normal distribution of residuals (α = 0.05) prior to conducting an ANOVA. Data not meeting these ANOVA assumptions were tested with a Wilcoxon or Kruskal–Wallis test. If ANOVAs indicated a difference, Tukey–Kramer HSD post-hoc tests were run to identify those treatment groups different from others. Pearson’s coefficient correlation analyses were run for data with normal distributions to assess potential in vivo predictive value of these in vitro screening approaches. Spearman’s coefficient correlation analysis was performed for data sets without a normal distribution. If a particle treatment elicited a low

number of significantly different cytokines compared to unexposed cells, correlation analysis was not conducted. All other data were analyzed with JMP SAS (version 13) software.

Results Physicochemical characterization of pre‑ and post‑incinerated nanoclays All particle characteristics in dry and culture medium suspension are summarized in Table 2. XRD and FESEM analyses indicated that both CloisNa and Clois30B were montmorillonite with dioctahedral structure and stacked platelet morphology. Clois30B displayed increased basal spacing compared to CloisNa indicative of the organic QAC coating (Fig.  1A, B; Table  2). Dispersed CloisNa in RPMI medium exhibited single or stacked platelet morphology similar to that observed in water (Fig.  2; Additional file  1: Figure S1). CloisNa showed the significantly smallest mean length and width (medians 294 and 174 nm) compared to all other particles (Additional file  3: Table  S3) with DLS size data matching FESEM data. CloisNa dispersed well (i.e. low PdI) and possessed the lowest ρEV of all particles tested (Table 2). Clois30B exhibited a range of size distributions, compared to CloisNa, and consisted of small sub-micron or large single micron stacked platelet morphology with size median of 304  nm. I-CloisNa possessed a smooth, amorphous quartz silicon oxide structure (Fig. 1B) with an electrondense, compacted appearance (Fig. 2). This differed from I-Clois30B’s quartz silicon oxide structure which exhibited morphologies including smooth, pocketed, [16, 17] and platelet-like structures, although at significantly larger sizes than Clois30B. Incinerated particles showed comparable sizes (mean width ranging 1636 ± 98 to 1731 ± 108 nm) with DLS data comparing to FESEM data. Incinerated nanoclays showed comparable ρEV ranging 1.26 to 1.39. Dispersed CS had a fractured, crystal-like morphology and displayed single micron size with comparable ρENM and ρEV to incinerated nanoclays. DLS hydrodynamic diameter was 40% smaller than FESEM width measurements. Zeta potentials were slightly negative (− 6.8 to − 10.3) with minimal changes in pH across all tested particles. Lastly, all endotoxin levels in particle stock suspensions were below the kit’s lower detection limit (Additional file 3: Table S4). Additional details on physicochemical characterization are presented in Supplemental Material.

The absence of an organic coating allowed for cooling silica oxide to form an amorphous quartz silicon oxide (i.e. I-CloisNa) [97] while presence of the organic coating allowed for some maintenance of a quartz structure (i.e. I-Clois30B) which follows previous findings [98, 99]. Following in  vivo exposure, large incinerated particulate with surrounding macrophage was observed in lung tissue while small endocytosed particulate was observed both in tissue and BALF cytospins [17]. Amorphous silica, such as I-CloisNa, possesses high inflammatory potential that is transient in nature with little persistent effect [14, 17]. I-CloisNa clearly displayed elevated inflammatory ability over I-Clois30B at equal high dose in non-LPS stimulated THP-1 cells with elevated levels of TNFα, IL-1β, IL-5, IL-17α, IL-15 and PDGF-ββ which matched in  vivo acute transient BALF inflammatory response, increased Caspase 1 cleavage, NF-κB, and Nrf2 expression in lung tissue [17]. I-Clois30B’s mixed morphology of amorphous and platelet-like silica [16, 18] produced a similar inflammatory cytokine profile compared to I-CloisNa, with both highly differing from CS. Interestingly, our finding that I-Clois30B crystal structure matches that of quartz further explains the increase in chronic inflammation in the in vivo model in concordance with the BALF cytokine profile and histopathology of CS-exposed animals. Crystalline silica was previously shown to cause acute mild inflammation and perturb macrophage phagocytosis and apoptosis that results in chronic inflammation and elevated risk of silicosis [14, 100]. The absence of CS effect following acute exposure is possibly due to the absence of reactive silanol groups on aged CS [14] and the retention of some amorphous silica particles within the I-Clois30B sample [16, 17]. Recent increased research into nanosized, surface coatings, vitreous, and sub-micron amorphous silica largely supports that amorphous surfaces can elicit acute inflammatory responses, but may exhibit reduced toxicity compared to uncoated, crystalline, or highly reactive surface chemistries [14, 101, 102]. The morphological and toxicodynamic similarities of I-Clois30B and CS, in the absence of the QAC coating, indicate the crystalline structure becomes the prevailing factor dictating chronic inflammatory response. This is juxtaposed to I-CloisNa with a pyrogenic amorphous structure and acute, but transient, inflammatory

effect. This indicates that prolonged incinerated ONC exposure represents a potential risk to long-term pulmonary health. In vitro to in vivo correlation analyses revealed that in  vitro model for human alveolar macrophage for cell viability, IL-1β release, and gasdermin D cleavage moderately to strongly aligned with in vivo BAL monocyte, neutrophil, and lymphocyte cell infiltrate counts on either Day 1 or Day 7 post-exposure. Furthermore, it supports the role of macrophages in the KE1 release of pro-inflammatory mediators driving KE2 increased recruitment of pro-inflammatory cells in the proposed lung fibrosis AOP. Some of the stronger correlations occurred with 3- or 10-fold increase in in  vitro dose above the in  vivo equivalent mass per area dose. This is not surprising since in vivo mass dose assumes that particles deposit entirely in the respiratory bronchi/ alveoli and homogeneously across the alveolar surface in the lung while assuming macrophages are not mobile. Since macrophages are mobile with a primary function to remove foreign material, it is expected that intracellular mass dose will be well above the local deposited mass dose. Next, non-LPS exposed macrophage cytokine profiles correlated with in vivo BAL profile (while LPS-stimulated macrophages did not) as both in vitro and in vivo hazard characterization studies are conducted in pathogen-free conditions with sterile particles. This analysis identified a five-cytokine profile (MIP1α, MIP1β, IL-8, TNFα, IL-6) for ONC that could be used in future nanoclay in vitro toxicity studies to screen for inflammatory effects. A previous ONC study also found in  vitro macrophage IL-8 expression correlated with their in vivo findings [26]. Lastly, several cytokines involved in ­TH2 cell recruitment and fibrosis (IL-6, eotaxin, PDGF-ββ, IL-10, IL-1β) were released from macrophages in vitro and correlated with in vivo BAL response, which aligns with KE4 ­(TH2 cell activation) in the lung fibrosis AOP. Collectively, this suggests in  vitro macrophage response assessment as an appropriate in  vitro screening tool for ONC lung toxicology research. Given the diversity of different morphologies and chemistries along nanoclay life cycles, traditional in vivo toxicity testing is not feasible. Here, we used a tiered screening strategy evaluating relationships between particle physicochemical properties and biological effect. Limitations to the study include uncertainty in deposited dose based on differences in effective density and heterogeneity in particle suspensions and how in vitro doses relate to unknown in  vivo deposited doses in the deep lung following known administered dose. Improvements to this approach can be developed to rapidly identify those nanoclays that pose elevated risk in occupational

Conclusions Herein, we evaluated two types of montmorillonite nanoclay and their incinerated byproducts for their toxicological and immunological profiles. We found clear evidence that physicochemical differences, namely presence/absence of QAC coating and incineration status, of nanoclays determines key events and molecular signaling patterns associated with lung macrophage inflammatory and cytotoxic responses. Further, we found correlations between toxicological and immunological effects observed in  vitro to those observed in a mouse model, adding to our understanding of ONC’s toxic mechanism along its life cycle and demonstrating the suitability of the in vitro non-LPS primed differentiated THP-1 model as a screening tool for nanoclays along their lifecycle.
